_readme: Spoken numbers in Relay's tier-1 languages, so a preacher can say the chapter
and verse in their own language: 'Yohana sura ya tatu, mstari wa kumi na sita'.
DATA, NOT RUST — same reason as book_aliases.json. A wrong numeral does not
fail safely: it silently shows a DIFFERENT VERSE. If 'tisa' were mapped to 8
instead of 9, nobody would notice until a service. A native speaker can correct
a number here in a one-line pull request without touching Rust.
THE GRAMMAR IS IN THE CODE; ONLY THE WORDS ARE HERE. The shape of these two
languages happens to be the same, which is why one state machine handles both:
tens + connector + ones     ishirini na tatu = 23   ashirin da uku = 23
ten  + connector + ones     kumi na tatu     = 13   goma sha uku   = 13
THE ONE THING THAT IS NOT LIKE ENGLISH, and it matters:
The hundred MULTIPLIER COMES AFTER the hundred word.
mia moja  = 100   (literally 'hundred one')   NOT 101
mia mbili = 200                               NOT 102
ɗari biyu = 200                               NOT 102
English puts it before ('two hundred'), so the English parser would have read
'mia mbili' as 100 + 2 = 102 and shown Psalm 102 when the preacher said 200.
`hundred_post` marks the words that behave this way.
A connector disambiguates: 'mia moja' (no connector) is 1×100, while
'mia na tatu' (connector) is 100+3. Both are handled.
Sources: Swahili — Omniglot / Languages and Numbers. Hausa — Omniglot /
Languages and Numbers / teachyourselfhausa.com.
YORÙBÁ (`yo`) DOES NOT USE THE STATE MACHINE ABOVE. Its numbers are single
vigesimal-subtractive words, so it carries `standalone` instead of ones/tens,
and it is marked `unreviewed` — nothing resolved through it may auto-fire.

sw._ones_note: kwanza/pili are the ORDINALS (first/second). 'mstari wa kwanza' = verse one — how a preacher actually says it. From 3 up, the ordinal and cardinal are the same word.
sw._linkers_note: Grammatical glue: 'sura YA tatu', 'mstari WA kwanza'. Skipped between a keyword and its number — never treated as numbers themselves.

ha._ones_note: farko/fari = 'first'. 'aya ta farko' = verse one. Hooked ɗ and ƙ fold to d and k automatically, so both spellings are safe to list.
ha._connectors_note: 'sha' builds the teens (goma sha uku = 13); 'da' joins tens and units (ashirin da uku = 23).

yo._status: UNREVIEWED BY A NATIVE SPEAKER. See `unreviewed` below.
yo._unreviewed_note: Every word in this block was authored without a native-speaker review, so a reference resolved through it is demoted to `UncertainNumber` and can never auto-fire — it is offered to the operator, who accepts it in one press. `docs/LANGUAGES.md` says the same thing in prose. Delete this flag when a Yorùbá speaker has checked the numbers, and the cap lifts by itself.
_shape_note: YORÙBÁ IS NOT SHAPED LIKE SWAHILI AND HAUSA, so it uses `standalone` and
neither `ones` nor `tens`. Yorùbá counting is vigesimal and subtractive:
16 is ẹrìndínlógún, 'four taken from twenty', ONE word. There is no
tens + connector + ones to run a state machine over. A `standalone` word IS
the whole number and combines with nothing, so a wrong entry can only ever
produce a wrong number where it stands — it can never silently change a
ONLY THE ORDINAL k- FORMS ARE LISTED, and that is a safety choice as much as
a usage one. A preacher says 'orí kẹta, ẹsẹ̀ kẹrìndínlógún' — the ordinal is
the register chapter and verse are actually spoken in. The bare cardinals are
left out because `normalize()` folds tone marks and dots-below, and several
of them then collide with ordinary sermon words: èje (7) and ẹ̀jẹ̀ (blood)
both fold to 'eje', and ogún (20), ògùn (medicine) and Ògún all fold to
'ogun'. That is rule 10's failure in another language, so those words are
Composite numbers above twenty (21 = ọ̀kànlélógún, 25 = ẹ̀ẹ́dọ́gbọ̀n) are
deliberately absent. They parse to nothing, which is exactly what they did
before this block existed — no regression, and no invented number.
yo._standalone_note: The ordinal k- forms for 1-20 and the round tens, plus the round tens as bare CARDINALS: a chapter of twenty or more is said 'orí ogún', not with a k- form. The bare units 1-9 are deliberately absent — that is where the homographs are once normalize() folds the tone marks (èje 7 / ẹ̀jẹ̀ blood, àrún 5 / àrùn disease, ẹ̀jọ 8 / ejò snake), and the k- ordinal already covers how a preacher says them. One collision is accepted and named: ogún (20) folds together with ògùn (medicine) and Ògún. It costs at most a SUGGESTION the operator ignores, because everything in this block is capped — see `unreviewed`. normalize() folds the tone marks and dots-below, so 'kẹrìndínlógún' and 'kerindinlogun' are one key and only one spelling has to be listed.
yo._words_note: 'orí kẹta' = chapter three; 'ẹsẹ̀ kẹrìndínlógún' = verse sixteen. Yorùbá needs no linker between the word and the number, so `linkers` is absent.
